lede: A boy who loved French books and the flute, beaten by a father who wanted a soldier, who grew up to be the most feared general in Europe and still played his flute every evening in his palace called 'without worries'.

ps: Frederick was born in Berlin on 24 January 1712, the son of King Frederick William I of Prussia. He ruled Prussia as Frederick II from 1740 until his death in 1786.

Months after he took the throne he invaded the rich Austrian province of Silesia and kept it through three wars. By the end of his reign small, scattered Prussia was one of the great powers of Europe.

He was also a writer, a flute player and a composer, who wrote in French, corresponded with Voltaire for decades and built the little palace of Sanssouci at Potsdam. Germans came to call him 'Old Fritz'.

His father was a hard, thrifty man obsessed with his army, known as the 'soldier king'. He despised his son's love of poetry, music and fine clothes, and beat and humiliated him, sometimes in front of others.

Frederick learned French culture from his tutor and his mother, Sophia Dorothea of Hanover. From 1728 the flautist Johann Joachim Quantz secretly gave him lessons, and his older sister Wilhelmine became his closest ally.

ps.t: In August 1730, aged eighteen, he tried to escape to England with his friend Hans Hermann von Katte. They were caught. On 6 November 1730 Katte was beheaded at the fortress of Küstrin, and Frederick was made to watch from a window.
ps.why: The trial and execution are documented in Prussian court records.

ps: After this he submitted. He worked in the provincial administration, married Princess Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Bevern in 1733 at his father's order, and spent happy years reading and making music at the castle of Rheinsberg. The marriage was cool and childless, and as king he lived apart from his wife.

1740: Anti-Machiavel, his reply to Machiavelli's The Prince, was published with Voltaire's help, arguing that a ruler must serve his people. The same year he became king on 31 May, and in December he marched into Silesia without a declaration of war.

1741 to 1745: the First and Second Silesian Wars against Maria Theresa of Austria. At his first battle, Mollwitz in 1741, he left the field believing it lost; his generals won it. He learned fast, and Austria had to give up Silesia.
1745 to 1747: Sanssouci was built on a terraced vineyard at Potsdam, a single-storey summer palace where he could read, write and play.

May 1747: the old Johann Sebastian Bach visited Potsdam, where his son Carl Philipp Emanuel was the king's harpsichordist. Frederick gave him a theme to improvise on, and Bach later wrote The Musical Offering on it.
1750 to 1753: Voltaire lived at his court. They quarrelled bitterly and Voltaire left, but they made up by letter later.

1756 to 1763: the Seven Years' War. Prussia faced Austria, France, Russia and Sweden together. He won famous victories at Rossbach and Leuthen in 1757, then was crushed by the Russians and Austrians at Kunersdorf in 1759, and Berlin was briefly occupied in 1760. The death of Empress Elizabeth of Russia in January 1762 saved him; her successor Peter III made peace. Prussia kept Silesia.

1772: with Russia and Austria he took part in the First Partition of Poland, seizing the land between Prussia and Brandenburg. Poland lost about a third of its territory to the three powers. After this he styled himself King of Prussia rather than King in Prussia.
17 August 1786: he died in his armchair at Sanssouci, aged 74.

He wrote a great deal, nearly all in French: histories of his own wars and house, poems, political testaments for his heirs, and thousands of letters. He thought German literature crude and said so in a 1780 essay.

ps.t: He composed about 120 flute sonatas and four flute concertos, and played chamber concerts most evenings for decades, until his teeth and breath failed him in old age.
ps.why: Totals vary between catalogues; the evening concerts are described by many visitors.

ps: Sanssouci, its terraces and its picture gallery, and the large New Palace at Potsdam, built after the Seven Years' War to show that Prussia was not ruined. They are now part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In his first days as king he largely abolished judicial torture and declared that in his lands everyone could be saved in his own way, meaning freedom of religion. That freedom had limits: Jews in Prussia lived under a harsh 1750 charter that restricted where they could live and how many children could settle.
Frederick William I (1688 to 1740), his father, who built the army Frederick used.
Wilhelmine of Bayreuth (1709 to 1758), his sister and lifelong confidante.
Hans Hermann von Katte (1704 to 1730), the friend executed for helping him flee.
Voltaire (1694 to 1778), the French writer, his correspondent, guest and sparring partner.
Johann Sebastian Bach (1685 to 1750), who played for him in 1747, and Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach (1714 to 1788), his court harpsichordist for nearly thirty years.
Johann Joachim Quantz (1697 to 1773), his flute teacher and court composer.
Maria Theresa of Austria (1717 to 1780), his great rival, who never forgave the loss of Silesia.
Catherine II of Russia (1729 to 1796), his partner in the partition of Poland.

This was the age of the Enlightenment, when writers argued that reason should guide government. Rulers like Frederick, Catherine II and Joseph II of Austria are called 'enlightened absolutists': they welcomed new ideas but kept all power in their own hands.

Wars were fought by professional armies drilled to march and fire in lines. Prussia, with a small population, kept one of the largest armies in Europe. It was said that Prussia was not a state with an army but an army with a state.
The Seven Years' War was fought across the world, in North America and India as well as Europe. Hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians died, and parts of Prussia were left devastated.
He left a larger, richer state with an efficient civil service and a formidable army. Prussia went on to unite Germany in 1871.
Later German nationalists made him a hero. In 1933 the Nazis staged the opening of Hitler's new parliament at the Garrison Church in Potsdam, where he was buried, to borrow his prestige.
He had asked to be buried on the terrace of Sanssouci near his dogs. That wish was finally carried out on 17 August 1991, after German reunification. Visitors still leave potatoes on his grave.

myths.c: He called himself 'the first servant of the state'.
myths.t: He wrote this idea several times, in French, including in his writings on government. He meant it, though he also ruled with no parliament to check him.

myths.c: He brought the potato to Prussia.
myths.t: Potatoes were already grown there. He pushed them hard: from 1756 he issued orders telling officials to make farmers plant them, as a defence against famine.

myths.c: A miracle saved him in the Seven Years' War.
myths.t: He spoke of the 'miracle of the House of Brandenburg' when his enemies failed to finish him after Kunersdorf in 1759. The phrase is now used most for 1762, when Empress Elizabeth's death took Russia out of the war.
Some contemporaries, including Voltaire, hinted so, and he had little interest in his wife. There is no firm evidence either way, and historians still disagree.
Sans souci is French for 'without care'. The name is written over the palace's central doors.
